title: Informal Letter Writing — personal letter format
notes: **What it is:** a letter to someone you know well — friend, family. Same skeleton, different temperature: warm, natural, personal.

**Block order:** Sender's address → Date → Salutation with first name ('Dear Rahul,') → Warm opening (ask about them / react to their letter) → Main body (news, invitation, reply) → Warm closing → 'Your loving friend,' + first name only.

**Tone grammar:** contractions welcome (it's, don't, I'm); question tags create warmth ('You remember that day, don't you?'); tenses mix naturally — past for news, present for feelings, future for plans.
**Exam check:** answer anything their last letter asked — examiners verify you responded; keep within ~130 words.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete informal letter template:**
[Your Address]
[City]
[Date: 15th March, 2025]

Dear [First Name],

Opening: Hope you're doing well / Thanks for your letter / Sorry for the delay.

Body paragraph 1: Respond to their news/questions (show you read their letter).

Body paragraph 2: Your news, invitation, or main message.

Body paragraph 3 (optional): Additional detail, feelings, or plans.

Closing: Looking forward to hearing from you / Can't wait to see you / Take care.

With love / Yours lovingly / Your loving friend,
[Your First Name Only]

**Opening strategies — warmth from the first line:** (1) *React to their letter*: 'I was so happy to hear about your promotion!' (2) *Apologise for delay*: 'Sorry I couldn't write sooner — exams kept me buried in books.' (3) *Ask about them*: 'How's the new job treating you? Still playing cricket on weekends?' (4) *Shared memory*: 'Walking past our old school yesterday reminded me of the time we…' (5) *General warmth*: 'Hope this letter finds you in the best of health and spirits.' Avoid: 'I am writing this letter to inform you…' — that's formal language.

**Body — natural conversation on paper:** Write as you speak, but with structure. Use paragraphs for different topics. Mix tenses naturally: 'I GOT the tickets (past) — we're GOING next month (future) — I'm SO EXCITED (present feeling).' Include sensory details: 'The mangoes here are incredibly sweet — you'd love them.' Use discourse markers: 'Anyway,', 'By the way,', 'Oh,', 'Guess what?', 'Actually,'. These create the feel of spoken English.

**Question tags and softeners — the warmth builders:** Question tags invite response: 'You're coming for Dashain, aren't you?' 'It's been ages since we met, hasn't it?' Softeners show consideration: 'I was wondering if you might…' 'Would you mind if…' 'I thought you'd like to know…' These small touches distinguish a personal letter from a formal one and earn expression marks.

**Closing — leave them wanting to reply:** (1) *Invitation to reply*: 'Do write back and tell me everything!' (2) *Future meeting*: 'Can't wait to catch up properly when you're in town.' (3) *Well-wishes*: 'Give my love to aunty and uncle. Take care of yourself.' (4) *Promise*: 'I'll send those photos I promised.' (5) *Emotional note*: 'Miss you loads.' Never end abruptly with just 'Bye' — the closing is your last impression.

**Sign-offs — the personal hierarchy:** Close friends/siblings: 'Love,' 'Lots of love,' 'Yours forever,'. Good friends: 'Your loving friend,' 'Yours truly,' 'Warm regards,'. Acquaintances/older relatives: 'With best wishes,' 'Yours affectionately,'. Parents/grandparents: 'Your loving son/daughter,' 'With love and respect,'. Match the sign-off to the relationship — examiners check this.

**Informal letter vocabulary — the natural register:** Formal → Informal shifts: 'I would like to invite you' → 'Come over!'; 'I am writing to inform you' → 'Just wanted you to know'; 'Please be advised' → 'Thought you should know'; 'I regret to inform you' → 'Bad news, I'm afraid'; 'Kindly respond' → 'Let me know'; 'I require' → 'I need'; 'It is requested' → 'Could you…'; 'We would be grateful' → 'We'd love it if…' Master these shifts — they're the heart of the informal register.

**Common informal letter exam tasks:** (1) *Reply to a friend's invitation* (accept/decline with reason). (2) *Invite a friend to an event* (birthday, wedding, picnic). (3) *Share personal news* (new job, exam results, moving house). (4) *Apologise for missing an event*. (5) *Give advice* (studying, career, relationships). (6) *Describe a visit/trip*. (7) *Congratulate on achievement*. (8) *Express sympathy/condolence*. Each has slightly different tone — practice all.

**Responding to their letter — the examiner's checklist:** Examiners explicitly check: Did you answer their questions? Did you acknowledge their news? Did you respond to their invitation? If their letter asked 'When are you coming?', your letter MUST say 'I'm coming on…' If they said 'I got the job!', you MUST congratulate them. Missing a response point loses content marks even if your English is perfect.

**Informal letter punctuation — relaxed but not sloppy:** Contractions use apostrophes (it's, don't, I'm, you're, we've). Exclamation marks are encouraged for excitement! 'Got the tickets!' Dashes and parentheses add conversational asides — 'The movie (you know, the one with the talking dog) was hilarious.' Ellipsis for trailing thoughts… 'I wonder if…' But: run-on sentences with only commas are still errors. Use full stops.

**Letter vs. Email vs. WhatsApp — register awareness:** In exams, 'informal letter' means the block format with address/date/salutation/body/close/signature. An 'informal email' adds To/Subject fields but keeps the warm body. A 'message/WhatsApp' is ultra-short, abbreviated, emoji-heavy. Don't confuse them. If the question says 'Write a letter to your friend…', use the full letter format even if you'd actually WhatsApp them in real life.

**Handwriting and presentation — the invisible marks:** While content and language are graded, legible handwriting, consistent margins, clear paragraph breaks, and correct spelling create a positive impression. Write the address and date on the right (traditional) or left (block) — be consistent. Leave a blank line between paragraphs. Don't cram — use the space. Examiners read hundreds of scripts; make yours easy to read.
confusion: Informal letter vs. Formal letter tone: Formal = 'I would be grateful if you could…' Informal = 'Could you…' or 'Can you…' Formal = 'I regret to inform you…' Informal = 'Sorry to say…' or 'Bad news…' The informal letter allows personality, emotion, and colloquialisms; the formal letter requires restraint, politeness, and standard English.

Dear Rahul, vs. Dear Sir/Madam,: The salutation signals the register. 'Dear [First Name],' = informal. 'Dear Sir/Madam,' = formal. 'Dear Mr. Sharma,' = formal (even if you know them professionally). In exams, if the prompt says 'your friend', use first name. If 'your principal', use 'Dear Sir/Madam,'. Mixing them confuses the register.

Yours lovingly vs. Yours faithfully: 'Yours faithfully' is ONLY for formal letters to strangers. 'Yours lovingly' / 'Your loving friend' / 'With love' are for informal letters. Using 'Yours faithfully' in a letter to your best friend is a major register error that costs marks.

Address placement — right vs. left: Traditional informal letters put sender's address on the TOP RIGHT. Modern block format puts it on the LEFT. Both are accepted in exams, but BE CONSISTENT — don't put address on right and date on left. Pick one style and use it throughout.

Replying to a letter vs. Writing a fresh letter: A reply MUST reference their letter ('Thanks for your letter…', 'Great to hear about…', 'Regarding your question about…'). A fresh letter (invitation, news) opens with a general warm opening. Examiners check for evidence of 'reading' their letter in a reply task.
practice: Write an informal letter (120-150 words) to your friend inviting them to spend the Dashain vacation with your family in your village. Include: specific dates, activities planned, what to bring, and a warm closing. Use at least 3 question tags and 2 contractions.

Write a reply letter (130-150 words) to a friend who wrote telling you they got admission to their dream university. Your letter must: congratulate them, ask 2 specific questions about the course, share your own current news, and suggest meeting to celebrate. Use natural informal tone throughout.

Write an informal letter (120-140 words) to your cousin apologising for missing their wedding. Explain the unavoidable reason, express regret, ask about the ceremony, and promise to visit soon. Include at least one softener ('I was wondering if…') and one discourse marker ('Anyway,').

Convert this formal sentence to informal: 'I would like to request your presence at the celebration of my birthday on the 25th of this month.' Then write a full informal invitation letter based on it.

Read the following letter from a friend and write a reply (130 words) that responds to EVERY point they raised: 'Hey! Just got back from the trek to Annapurna Base Camp — incredible views! How are your board prep exams going? Still playing guitar? Let's plan a trip together after exams. Write soon!'
universalFacts: The informal letter as a distinct genre emerged in the 18th century with the rise of the postal system and the middle class. Before that, most personal communication was face-to-face or through messengers. The 'penny post' (1840) made letter-writing affordable for ordinary people.

In the NEB English exam, informal letter writing typically carries 5-8 marks. The marking breakdown: Format (2 marks), Content/Response (3 marks), Expression/Tone (3 marks). The 'response' criterion is unique to informal letters — you MUST show you read and answered their letter.

Jane Austen's novels (Pride and Prejudice, Emma) feature letters as major plot devices. Characters reveal their true selves in letters — the informal letter was considered the most honest form of communication. This literary tradition influences how we value 'personal voice' in letter writing today.

The phrase 'P.S.' (postscript) comes from Latin 'post scriptum' (written after). In informal letters, the P.S. is where the most personal, spontaneous, or afterthought content lives — often the most genuine part. In exams, a well-placed P.S. can add warmth: 'P.S. Found that photo of us from 2010 — sending it along!'

Research on epistolary (letter-based) communication shows that people disclose more personal information in letters than in face-to-face conversations. The physical act of writing, the privacy, and the time delay create psychological safety. This is why informal letters remain powerful for emotional connection even in the digital age.
